newsitem.title: USA: Yahoo raising its advertising rates - CFO.
newsitem.headline: Yahoo raising its advertising rates - CFO.

text.p: Yahoo! Inc. Chief Financial Officer Gary Valenzuela said on Monday the Internet service's advertising rates were inching upward, particulary on new speciality products aimed at children and other niche audiences.

Valenzuela also told investors at a conference sponsored by Robert James & Associaties Inc that Yahoo!, best known for its Internet directory and search service, was posting revenue gains but cautioned that the company was unlikely to maintain the very strong pace of year-over-year revenue gains posted in the fourth quarter and full year of 1996.
The executive also said the company had a $102 million cash reserve, which might be used for acquisitions.
"We are in a position to be opportunistic, and we will be," Valenzuela said.
He gave no details of possible acquisitions.
Yahoo! computer servers had 20 million information requests in December, 1996, and roughly one of every four Yahoo! responses carried a paid banner advertisement, he said.
The company was getting about two to six cents per advertisement viewing, Valenzuela said.

The rate was slightly higher for Yahoo! services aimed at investors, children and non-U.S. markets, he said. The range on the speciality services tended to be four to seven cents per advertisement viewing, he said.
Traffic at Yahoo! sites increased in January over December, he said.

But Valenzuela said the company's revenues may mimic those of more established media, such as broadcast television and newspapers, and show first-quarter sluggishness after the Christmas shopping season. "It is too early to say," he said.
The company's 1996 revenues, derived almost entirely from advertising, jumped 1,200 percent to $19.1 million over 1995 levels.
Raymond James forecasts Yahoo! sales will double in 1997 to about $40 million and rise again in 1998 to $70 million.

Yahoo! is expected to report a small per share loss for the first quarter, when the company reports in early May, according to a First Call survey of Wall Street analysts. Estimates range from zero to a four cent per share loss.
The company in its 1996 first quarter had no per-share earnings.
